title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — Second Congress at Lacedaemon—Preparations for War and Diplomatic Skirmishes—Cylon—Pausanias—Themistocles
paragraphs: Not many years after this, we come at last to the events already related: the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the incidents that served as a pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes, against each other and against the barbarian, took place in the fifty years between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of this war. In that time the Athenians put their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians saw it clearly, yet opposed it only briefly and for the most part stayed inactive. They were slow by long habit to go to war unless necessity forced them, and in this case they were also hampered by wars at home. At last the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy came under its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer. The time had come to throw themselves heart and soul upon the hostile power and break it, if they could, by beginning the present war. They had already made up their own minds that the treaty had been broken and that the Athenians were guilty. Even so, they sent to Delphi and asked the God whether war would be well for them. As it is reported, he answered that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and he promised that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or uninvoked. Still, they wished to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether it was proper to make war. The ambassadors of the confederates arrived and a congress was convened. All spoke their minds, and most of them denounced the Athenians and demanded that the war begin. The Corinthians did so in particular. Earlier they had gone through the cities one by one on their own account, urging them to vote for war, for fear that it would come too late to save Potidæa. They were present on this occasion too, and they came forward last and spoke as follows:

“Fellow allies, we can no longer accuse the Lacedaemonians of failing in their duty. They have not only voted for war themselves, but have gathered us here for that purpose. We say their duty, because supremacy has its duties. Leaders must administer private interests fairly, but they must also show special care for the common welfare, in return for the special honors that all pay them in other ways. As for ourselves, those who have already had dealings with the Athenians need no warning to be on their guard against them. The states farther inland, away from the main routes of communication, should understand that if they fail to support the coast powers, they will damage the passage of their own produce down to the sea for export, and the reception in exchange of imports from the sea. They must not judge what is said here carelessly, as if it did not concern them. They must expect that if the coast powers are sacrificed, the danger will one day reach the interior too, and they must recognize that their own interests are deeply involved in this discussion. For these reasons they should not hesitate to exchange peace for war. Wise men stay quiet as long as they are not injured, but brave men leave peace for war when they are injured, and return to an understanding when a favorable opportunity comes. They are neither intoxicated by success in war nor willing to take an injury for the sake of the pleasant tranquillity of peace. Indeed, if you stay inactive, to hesitate for the sake of such pleasures is the quickest way to lose the sweets of repose to which you cling. And to conceive extravagant pretensions from success in war is to forget how hollow is the confidence that elates you. Many ill-conceived plans have succeeded because their opponents were still more foolish, but many more that seemed well laid have ended in disgrace. The confidence with which we form our schemes is never fully justified in their execution. Speculation is carried on in safety, but when it comes to action, fear causes failure.

“To apply these rules to ourselves: if we are kindling war now, we do so under the pressure of injury and with adequate grounds of complaint, and when we have chastised the Athenians we will stop in due season. We have many reasons to expect success. First, we are superior in numbers and in military experience. Second, we are generally and unfailingly obedient in carrying out orders. As for naval strength, which they possess, we shall build it up from the resources each of us already has and from the moneys at Olympia and Delphi. A loan from these will enable us to lure away their foreign sailors by offering higher pay. For the power of Athens is bought rather than national, while ours will not run the same risk, since its strength lies more in men than in money. A single defeat at sea will in all likelihood ruin them. If they hold out, we shall have the more time to train ourselves in naval matters, and as soon as we have reached equality in skill, we need hardly ask whether we shall be their superiors in courage. For the advantages we have by nature they cannot acquire by education, while their superiority in skill we can remove by practice. The money required for these purposes shall be provided by our contributions. Nothing could be more monstrous than to suggest that, while their allies never tire of contributing toward their own servitude, we should refuse to spend on vengeance and self-preservation the treasure that, by refusing, we shall lose to Athenian rapacity and see used for our own ruin.

“We have other ways of carrying on the war as well: the revolt of their allies, which is the surest way of depriving them of the revenues that are the source of their strength; the establishment of fortified positions in their country; and various operations that cannot be foreseen at present. For of all things war proceeds least by definite rules. It draws mainly on itself for devices to meet an emergency, and in such cases the party that faces the struggle and keeps his temper best finds the most security, while the one who loses his temper finds corresponding disaster. Let us also reflect that if this were merely a series of territorial disputes between rival neighbors, it might be borne. But in Athens we have an enemy that is a match for our whole coalition and more than a match for any one of its members. Unless we make a united stand against her, as a body and as individual nations and cities, she will easily conquer us when we are divided and take us one by one. That conquest, terrible as it may sound, would, it must be understood, have no other end than slavery pure and simple. Peloponnese cannot even hear that word whispered without disgrace, nor see so many states abused by one without disgrace. Meanwhile people would conclude either that we were justly treated so, or that we put up with it out of cowardice and were proving ourselves degenerate sons, since we would not even secure for ourselves the freedom that our fathers gave to Hellas. We would be allowing a tyrant state to be established in Hellas, though in individual states we think it our duty to put down sole rulers. We do not know how this conduct can be held free from three of the gravest failings: want of sense, want of courage, or want of vigilance. For we do not suppose that you have taken refuge in that contempt of an enemy which has proved so fatal in so many instances, a feeling which has ruined so many that it has come to be called not contemptuous but contemptible.

“There is, however, no advantage in reflecting on the past beyond what may serve the present. For the future we must provide by holding on to what the present gives us and redoubling our efforts. It is hereditary with us to win virtue as the fruit of labor, and you must not change the habit, even if you now have a slight advantage in wealth and resources. For it is not right that what was won in want should be lost in plenty. No, we must advance boldly to the war, for many reasons. The god has commanded it and promised to be with us, and the rest of Hellas will join the struggle, some from fear, some from interest. You will not be the first to break a treaty, since the god, in advising us to go to war, judges it to be violated already. Rather you will be supporting a treaty that has been outraged. Indeed, treaties are broken not by resistance but by aggression.

“Your position, therefore, from whatever side you view it, will amply justify you in going to war. We recommend this step in the interests of all, bearing in mind that identity of interest is the surest of bonds, whether between states or between individuals. Do not delay, then, to help Potidæa, a Dorian city besieged by Ionians, which is quite a reversal of the proper order of things, nor to assert the freedom of the rest. We cannot wait any longer when waiting can only mean immediate disaster for some of us, and, if it becomes known that we have conferred but do not venture to protect ourselves, like disaster in the near future for the rest. Do not delay, fellow allies. Be convinced of the necessity of the crisis and the wisdom of this counsel, and vote for the war. Do not be deterred by its immediate terrors, but look beyond them to the lasting peace that will follow. Out of war peace gains fresh stability, but refusing to leave repose for war is not so sure a way of avoiding danger. We must believe that the tyrant city established in Hellas has been established against all alike, with a program of universal empire, part fulfilled and part in contemplation. Let us then attack and reduce it, and win future security for ourselves and freedom for the Hellenes who are now enslaved.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. The Lacedaemonians had now heard all the opinions. They took the vote of all the allied states present in order, great and small alike, and the majority voted for war. This was decided, but it was still impossible for them to begin at once, since they were unprepared. It was resolved that the different states should procure the means required, and that there should be no delay. And indeed, despite the time taken up by the necessary arrangements, less than a year passed before Attica was invaded and the war openly begun.

This interval was spent in sending embassies to Athens with complaints, in order to have as good a pretext for war as possible if she paid no attention to them. The first Lacedaemonian embassy ordered the Athenians to drive out the curse of the goddess. Its history is as follows. In former generations there was an Athenian named Cylon, a victor at the Olympic games, of good birth and powerful position, who had married a daughter of Theagenes, a Megarian who was then tyrant of Megara. Now Cylon was consulting the oracle at Delphi, and the god told him to seize the Acropolis of Athens on the grand festival of Zeus. So he obtained a force from Theagenes and persuaded his friends to join him. When the Olympic festival in Peloponnese came, he seized the Acropolis, intending to make himself tyrant. He thought this was the grand festival of Zeus, and also an occasion fitting for an Olympic victor. Whether the grand festival that was meant was in Attica or elsewhere, he never considered, and the oracle did not offer to settle. For the Athenians also have a festival called the grand festival of Zeus Meilichios or Gracious, namely the Diasia. It is celebrated outside the city, and the whole people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the country. However, believing he had chosen the right time, he made the attempt. As soon as the Athenians noticed it, they flocked in from the country, one and all, sat down, and laid siege to the citadel. But as time went on, most of them grew weary of the labor of the blockade and departed. The responsibility of keeping guard was left to the nine archons, with full powers to arrange everything as they judged best. It must be known that at that time most political functions were discharged by the nine archons. Meanwhile Cylon and his besieged companions were suffering from want of food and water. Cylon and his brother made their escape, but the rest were hard pressed, and some were even dying of famine, so they seated themselves as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis. The Athenians who had been charged with keeping guard saw them at the point of death in the temple. They raised them up on the understanding that no harm should be done to them, led them out, and killed them. Some who took refuge at the altars of the awful goddesses as they passed by were dispatched on the spot. For this deed the men who killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess, they and their descendants. So these accursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, and driven out again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction. The living were driven out, and the bones of the dead were taken up, and thus they were cast out. For all that, they came back afterwards, and their descendants are still in the city.

This, then, was the curse that the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out. As they pretended, they were motivated chiefly by concern for the honor of the gods. But they also knew that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side, and they thought that his banishment would greatly advance their designs on Athens. They did not really hope to bring this about. They thought rather to create a prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen, who would feel that the war was partly caused by his misfortune. For he was the most powerful man of his time and the leading Athenian statesman. He opposed the Lacedaemonians in everything, would allow no concessions, and constantly urged the Athenians on to war.

The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of Taenarus. The Lacedaemonians had once raised some Helot suppliants up from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away and killed them, and they believe the great earthquake at Sparta to have been a retribution for it. The Athenians also ordered them to drive out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House. Its history is as follows. Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this was his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted. He was not sent out again in a public capacity, but he took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without the authority of the Lacedaemonians, and arrived in the Hellespont as a private person. He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, but really to carry on his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, since he was ambitious of reigning over Hellas. What first enabled him to put the King under an obligation, and to make a beginning of the whole design, was this. Some connections and kinsmen of the King had been taken in Byzantium when it was captured from the Medes, during his first stay there, after the return from Cyprus. He sent these captives off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, giving out that they had escaped from him. He managed this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had put in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners. He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which, as was discovered afterwards, were as follows: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, wishing to do you a favor, sends you these prisoners of war. I also propose, with your approval, to marry your daughter, and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. I may say that I think I am able to do this, with your co-operation. So if any of this pleases you, send a trustworthy man to the sea, through whom we may conduct our correspondence in future.”

This was all that the writing revealed, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter. He sent Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea, with orders to replace Megabates, the previous governor in the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send over to Pausanias at Byzantium as quickly as possible a letter that he entrusted to him. Artabazus was to show Pausanias the royal signet, and to carry out with all care and fidelity any commission he might receive from Pausanias on the King’s business. When Artabazus arrived, he carried out the King’s orders and sent over the letter, which contained the following answer: “Thus says King Xerxes to Pausanias. For the men whom you have saved for me across the sea from Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded for ever, and I am well pleased with your proposals. Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing any of your promises to me. Do not let them be hindered by the cost of gold or silver, nor by the number of troops, wherever their presence may be needed. With Artabazus, an honorable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, in whatever way may be most to the honor and interest of us both.”

Pausanias had earlier been held in high honor by the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea. After he received this letter he became prouder than ever and could no longer live in the usual style. He left Byzantium in a Median dress and was attended on his march through Thrace by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians. He kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to hide his intentions, but betrayed in trifles what his ambition one day meant to enact on a grander scale. He also made himself hard to approach and showed such a violent temper to everyone without exception that no one could come near him. Indeed, this was the principal reason why the confederacy went over to the Athenians.

When this conduct came to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, it caused his first recall. After his second voyage out in the ship of Hermione, without their orders, he gave proofs of similar behavior. He was besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the Athenians, and did not return to Sparta. News came that he had settled at Colonae in the Troad and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good purpose. The ephors, no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy. He was anxious above everything to avoid suspicion, and confident that he could quash the charge with money, so he returned to Sparta a second time. At first the ephors threw him into prison (their powers enable them to do this to the King). Soon he settled the matter and came out again, and offered himself for trial to anyone who wished to bring an inquiry against him.

Now the Spartans, whether his enemies or the nation at large, had no tangible proof against him, of the indubitable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family who was at that moment in high office. He was regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus, Leonidas’s son, who was still a minor. But his contempt for the laws and his imitation of the barbarians gave grounds for much suspicion that he was discontented with the established order. They reviewed all the occasions on which he had in any way departed from the regular customs, and remembered that he had taken it upon himself to have the following couplet inscribed on the tripod at Delphi, which was dedicated by the Hellenes as the first-fruits of the spoil of the Medes:
The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised This monument, that Phœbus might be praised.

At the time the Lacedaemonians had at once erased the couplet and inscribed the names of the cities that had helped overthrow the barbarian and had dedicated the offering. Yet it was considered that Pausanias had been guilty of a grave offense here, and in the light of the attitude he had since taken, it gained a new significance and seemed quite in keeping with his present schemes. Besides, they were informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots. Such indeed was the fact, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in insurrection and help him carry out his plans to the end. Even now the ephors mistrusted the evidence even of the Helots themselves and would not consent to take any decided step against him. They were following their regular custom toward themselves, which is to be slow in taking any irrevocable resolve concerning a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof. At last, it is said, the man who was going to carry the last letter for the King to Artabazus turned informer. He was a man of Argilus, once the favorite and most trusted servant of Pausanias. He was alarmed by the reflection that none of the previous messengers had ever returned. So he counterfeited the seal, in order that, if he found himself mistaken in his surmises, or if Pausanias should ask to make some correction, he would not be discovered. Then he undid the letter and found the postscript he had suspected, namely an order to put him to death.

The ephors were shown the letter and now felt more certain. Still, they wished to hear Pausanias commit himself with their own ears. So the man went by appointment to Taenarus as a suppliant, and there built himself a hut divided in two by a partition. Inside it he concealed some of the ephors and let them hear the whole matter plainly. For Pausanias came to him and asked the reason for his position as a suppliant. The man reproached him with the order that he had written concerning him, and declared one by one all the other circumstances: how he had never yet brought Pausanias into any danger while employed as agent between him and the King, and yet, like the mass of his servants, was to be rewarded with death. Pausanias admitted all this, told him not to be angry about it, gave him a pledge of raising him up from the temple, and begged him to set off as quickly as possible and not to hinder the business in hand.

The ephors listened carefully and then departed. They took no action for the moment, but, having at last attained certainty, were preparing to arrest him in the city. It is reported that as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors what he was coming for. Another, too, made him a secret signal and betrayed it to him out of kindness. He set off running for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, whose enclosure was near at hand, and took sanctuary before they could seize him. He entered a small chamber that formed part of the temple, to avoid being exposed to the weather, and lay still there. The ephors, for the moment outdistanced in the pursuit, afterwards took the roof off the chamber, made sure that he was inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and stayed before the place, reducing him by starvation. When they found that he was on the point of expiring, just as he was in the chamber, they brought him out of the temple while the breath was still in him, and as soon as he was brought out he died. They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they cast criminals, but finally decided to bury him somewhere nearby. But the god at Delphi afterwards ordered the Lacedaemonians to move the tomb to the place of his death, where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares. Since what had been done was a curse upon them, he also ordered them to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House. So they had two brazen statues made and dedicated them as a substitute for Pausanias. The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians to drive out what the god himself had pronounced to be a curse.

To return to the Medism of Pausanias. In the course of the inquiry, material was found that implicated Themistocles, and the Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians and required them to punish him as they had punished Pausanias. The Athenians consented to do so. But he had, as it happened, been ostracized, and, while living at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of Peloponnese. So they sent persons with instructions to take him wherever they found him, accompanied by the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join in the pursuit. But Themistocles got wind of their intentions and fled from Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations to him. But the Corcyraeans said they could not venture to shelter him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the mainland opposite. The officers who hung on the reports of his movements pursued him, and at a loss where to turn, he was compelled to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms. Admetus happened not to be indoors, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth. Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was. He begged him not to take revenge on Themistocles in exile for any opposition that Admetus’s requests might have met from Themistocles at Athens. Indeed, he was now far too low for his revenge, he said, since retaliation was honorable only between equals. Besides, his opposition to the king had affected only the success of a request, not the safety of his person. If the king were to give him up to the pursuers he had mentioned, and to the fate they intended for him, he would simply be consigning him to certain death.

The King listened to him and raised him up, with his son, as he was sitting with him in his arms in the most effective form of supplication. When the Lacedaemonians arrived not long afterwards, he refused to give Themistocles up for anything they could say. Instead he sent him off by land to the other sea, to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, since Themistocles wished to go to the Persian king. There he met a merchant ship on the point of starting for Ionia. He went on board and was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron that was blockading Naxos. In his alarm — luckily he was unknown to the people in the vessel — he told the master who he was and what he was fleeing from. He said that if the master refused to save him, he would declare that he was taking him for a bribe. Meanwhile their safety lay in letting no one leave the ship until a favorable time for sailing should arise. If the master complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper recompense. The master did as he asked, and after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, at length arrived at Ephesus.

After rewarding him with a present of money, Themistocles, as soon as he had received funds from his friends at Athens and from his secret hoards at Argos, started for the interior with one of the coast Persians and sent a letter to King Artaxerxes, the son of Xerxes, who had just come to the throne. It read as follows: “I, Themistocles, have come to you. Of all the Hellenes I did your house the most harm, when I was compelled to defend myself against your father’s invasion — but the good I did him during his retreat far outweighed it, for that brought no danger to me and great danger to him. For the past, you owe me a good turn” — here he mentioned the warning sent to Xerxes from Salamis to retreat, and his finding the bridges unbroken, which he falsely pretended was due to him — “and for the present I am here, able to do you great service, pursued by the Hellenes for my friendship for you. However, I ask a year’s grace, after which I shall be able to declare in person the objects of my coming.”

It is said that the King approved his intention and told him to do as he said. Themistocles used the interval to make what progress he could in the Persian language and in the customs of the country. When he arrived at court at the end of the year, he rose to very high standing there, higher than any Hellene has ever held before or since. This was partly because of his splendid past, partly because of the hopes he held out of subjugating Hellas for the King, but principally because of the proof of his ability that experience gave daily. For Themistocles was a man who showed the clearest signs of genius, and in this respect he has a claim on our admiration that is quite extraordinary and unparalleled. By his own native ability, which he had neither developed nor supplemented by study, he was at once the best judge in those sudden crises that allow little or no deliberation, and the best prophet of the future, even in its most distant possibilities. He could expound well whatever came within the range of his practice, and he was still able to form an adequate judgment in matters in which he had no experience. He could also divine excellently the good and evil hidden in the unseen future. In short, whether we consider the extent of his natural powers or the slightness of his application, this extraordinary man must be allowed to have surpassed all others in the faculty of meeting an emergency by intuition. Disease was the real cause of his death, though there is a story that he ended his life by poison, on finding himself unable to fulfill his promises to the King. However that may be, there is a monument to him in the marketplace of Asiatic Magnesia. He was governor of the district: the King had given him Magnesia, which brought in fifty talents a year, to supply his bread, Lampsacus, which was considered the richest wine country, to supply his wine, and Myos to supply other provisions. His bones, it is said, were brought home by his relatives in accordance with his wishes and buried in Attic ground. This was done without the knowledge of the Athenians, since the law forbids burying in Attica an outlaw for treason. So ends the history of Pausanias and Themistocles, the Lacedaemonian and the Athenian, the most famous men of their time in Hellas.

To return to the Lacedaemonians. Their first embassy, with its demands and the reply it provoked concerning the expulsion of the accursed persons, has already been related. A second embassy followed. It ordered Athens to raise the siege of Potidæa and to respect the independence of Aegina. Above all, it made plain that war could be prevented if the Megara decree were revoked, the decree that shut the Megarians out of Athenian harbors and out of the market of Athens. But Athens was unwilling either to revoke the decree or to consider their other proposals. She accused the Megarians of pushing their cultivation into the consecrated ground and the unenclosed land on the border, and of harboring her runaway slaves. At last an embassy arrived with the Lacedaemonian ultimatum. The ambassadors were Ramphias, Melesippus, and Agesander. Not a word was said on any of the old subjects. There was simply this: “Lacedaemon wishes the peace to continue, and there is no reason why it should not, if you would leave the Hellenes independent.” Upon this the Athenians held an assembly and laid the matter before it. They resolved to deliberate once for all on all the Lacedaemonian demands and give an answer. Many speakers came forward and supported one side or the other. Some urged the necessity of war, others the revocation of the decree and the folly of letting it stand in the way of peace. Among them was Pericles, son of Xanthippus, the first man of his time at Athens, ablest alike in counsel and in action, who came forward and gave the following advice:

“There is one principle, Athenians, that I hold to through everything: no concession to the Peloponnesians. I know that the spirit that inspires men while they are being persuaded to make war is not always kept once they act, and that resolutions change as circumstances change. Yet I see that now, as before, the same counsel is demanded of me, almost literally the same. And I put it to those of you who are allowing yourselves to be persuaded: support the national resolves even if we meet with reverses, or else give up all credit for their wisdom if we succeed. For sometimes the course of events is as arbitrary as the plans of men; indeed this is why we usually blame chance for whatever does not happen as we expected. Now it was clear before that Lacedaemon entertained designs against us, and it is still clearer now. The treaty provides that we shall submit our differences to each other for legal settlement and that meanwhile each shall keep what it has. Yet the Lacedaemonians have never made us any such offer and have never accepted one from us. On the contrary, they wish complaints to be settled by war instead of by negotiation, and in the end we find them here dropping the tone of expostulation and adopting that of command. They order us to raise the siege of Potidæa, to let Aegina be independent, and to revoke the Megara decree, and they conclude with an ultimatum warning us to leave the Hellenes independent. I hope none of you will think that we shall be going to war for a trifle if we refuse to revoke the Megara decree. It stands in front of their complaints, and its revocation is supposed to save us from war. I hope, too, that no feeling of self-reproach will linger in your minds, as if you went to war for slight cause. Why, this trifle contains the whole seal and trial of your resolution. If you give way, you will instantly have to meet some greater demand, since you will have been frightened into obedience in the first instance, whereas a firm refusal will make them understand clearly that they must treat you more as equals. Make your decision therefore at once: either submit before you are harmed, or, if we are to go to war, as I for one think we ought, do so without caring whether the ostensible cause is great or small, resolved against making concessions and against consenting to a precarious tenure of our possessions. For every claim from an equal, urged upon a neighbor as a command before any attempt at legal settlement, whether great or small, has only one meaning, and that is slavery.

“As to the war and the resources of either side, a detailed comparison will show you that Athens is not the inferior. The Peloponnesians work their own land, and they have no funds, private or public. They are also without experience in long wars across the sea, because the poverty that limits their attacks on each other keeps them to short campaigns. Powers of this description are quite incapable of manning a fleet or sending out an army often: they cannot afford to be away from their homes and to spend from their own funds, and besides, they do not command the sea. Capital, it must be remembered, sustains a war better than forced contributions do. Farmers are always more ready to serve in person than in purse. They are confident that they will survive the dangers, but by no means sure that their money will not be exhausted prematurely, especially if the war lasts longer than they expect, as it very likely will. In a single battle the Peloponnesians and their allies may be able to defy all Hellas, but they are incapable of carrying on a war against a power different in character from their own. They lack the single council-chamber required for prompt and vigorous action, and in its place have a diet composed of various races, in which every state has an equal vote and each presses its own ends, a condition that generally results in no action at all. The great wish of some is to avenge themselves on a particular enemy, the great wish of others to save their own pockets. They are slow in assembling, and they devote a very small fraction of the time to any public object and most of it to their own affairs. Meanwhile each fancies that no harm will come of his neglect and that it is somebody else’s business to look after this or that for him. So, since all separately entertain the same notion, the common cause decays without anyone noticing.

“But the principal point is the hindrance that want of money will cause them. Money comes in slowly, so they will be delayed, and the opportunities of war wait for no man. Again, we need not be alarmed at the possibility of their building fortifications in Attica, or at their navy. Even in time of peace it would be hard for any system of fortifications to set up a rival city, and surely much harder in an enemy’s country, when Athens is fortified against it just as much as it is against Athens. A mere outpost could do some harm to the country through raids and by making desertion easy, but it can never stop us from sailing into their country, building fortifications there, and making reprisals with our powerful fleet. For our skill at sea helps us more on land than their skill on land helps them at sea. They will not find familiarity with the sea easy to acquire. You have practiced it ever since the Median invasion and have not yet brought it to perfection. Is there any chance, then, that an agricultural population with no seafaring, who will besides be kept from practicing by strong squadrons of observation from Athens always on watch, will achieve anything considerable? With a small squadron they might risk an engagement, encouraging their ignorance with numbers. But a strong force confronting them will keep them from moving, and for want of practice they will grow more clumsy and therefore more timid. It must be kept in mind that seamanship, just like anything else, is a matter of art. It cannot be taken up now and then as a pastime for times of leisure. On the contrary, it is so exacting that it leaves leisure for nothing else.

“Suppose they were to touch the moneys at Olympia or Delphi and try to tempt our foreign sailors away with higher pay. That would be a serious danger only if we could not still match them by putting our own citizens and the resident aliens aboard. In fact we can always do so. And best of all, among our own citizens we have more native coxswains and sailors, and of a higher class, than all the rest of Hellas put together. Besides, to say nothing of the risk involved, none of our foreign sailors would agree to become an outlaw from his own country and join them and their hopes for the sake of a few days’ high pay.

“This, I think, is a fairly accurate account of the position of the Peloponnesians. Athens has none of the defects I have criticized in them, and has other advantages that they can show nothing to equal. If they march against our country, we will sail against theirs. It will then turn out that the devastation of all Attica is not comparable to that of even a fraction of Peloponnese, for they can make good the loss only by a battle, while we have plenty of land both on the islands and on the continent. Rule of the sea is indeed a great matter. Think for a moment. If we were islanders, could you imagine a more impregnable position? Well, from now on we should, as far as possible, think of our position in just that way. We must put all thought of our land and houses aside and keep careful watch over the sea and the city. However irritated we may be over the land and houses, we must not let it provoke us into a battle with the Peloponnesians, who outnumber us. If we won, we should only have to fight another battle against the same superiority. If we lost, we should lose our allies, the source of our strength, and they will not stay quiet a day once we are unable to march against them. Our tears should be shed not for houses and land but for men’s lives, since houses and land do not gain men, but men gain them. And if I thought I could persuade you, I would tell you to go out and lay them waste with your own hands, and so show the Peloponnesians that this at any rate will not make you submit.

“I have many other reasons to hope for a favorable outcome, provided that you can agree not to add schemes of fresh conquest to the conduct of the war, and will not deliberately bring other dangers on yourselves. Indeed, I fear our own blunders more than the enemy’s devices. But these matters shall be explained in another speech, when events require it. For the present, send these men away with this answer. We will let Megara use our market and harbors when the Lacedaemonians stop their alien acts against us and our allies, since nothing in the treaty forbids either one or the other. We will leave the cities independent, if they were independent when we made the treaty, and when the Lacedaemonians give their own cities an independence that does not mean subservience to Lacedaemonian interests, but is whatever each severally may desire. We are willing to give the legal satisfaction that our agreements specify. We shall not begin hostilities, but we shall resist those who do. This answer is agreeable at once to the rights and the dignity of Athens. It must be thoroughly understood that war is a necessity. But the more readily we accept it, the less eager our opponents will be, and out of the greatest dangers communities and individuals win the greatest glory. Our fathers resisted the Medes, did they not, with resources far different from ours, and even after those resources had been abandoned? And more by wisdom than by fortune, more by daring than by strength, did they not beat off the barbarian and bring their affairs to their present height? We must not fall behind them. We must resist our enemies in any way and in every way, and try to hand down our power to our posterity unimpaired.”

Such were the words of Pericles. The Athenians were persuaded that his advice was wise, and they voted as he wished. They gave the Lacedaemonians the answer he recommended, on the separate points and on the whole: they would do nothing on dictation, but were ready to have the complaints settled fairly and impartially by the legal method that the terms of the truce prescribed. The envoys then went home, and they did not come again.

These were the charges and differences between the rival powers before the war, which arose immediately from the affair at Epidamnus and Corcyra. Even so, intercourse and mutual communication went on. It was carried on without heralds, though not without suspicion, because events were happening that amounted to a breach of the treaty and gave grounds for war.
